The Accounting Equation: Accounting
The system of recording, classifying, and reporting financial activity
Accounting equation
Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity
Asset
A resource owned by a business that has value
Liability
A debt or obligation the business owes to outsiders
Owner's equity
The owner's claim on the assets after liabilities are paid
Capital account
The equity account recording the owner's investment
Drawing account
The account recording owner withdrawals for personal use
Business entity concept
Treating the business as separate from its owner
Going concern assumption
Assuming the business will continue operating indefinitely
Accounts receivable
Money customers owe the business
Accounts payable
Money the business owes to suppliers
Revenue and expense effect on equity
Revenue increases equity while expenses decrease it
Analyzing Transactions: Transaction
Any business event that changes the accounting equation
Source document
The original paperwork proving a transaction occurred
Invoice
A document billing a customer for goods or services
Receipt
A document confirming that cash was received
Memorandum
An internal document describing a transaction
Dual effect of transactions
Every transaction affects at least two accounts
Chart of accounts
The organised list of all accounts a business uses
Account title
The name identifying what an account tracks
Purchase on account
Acquiring an asset now and agreeing to pay later
Payment on account
Reducing both cash and accounts payable
Revenue transaction
A sale that increases assets and increases equity
Expense transaction
A cost that decreases assets or increases liabilities and reduces equity
Debits and Credits: An entry recorded on the left side of an account
An entry recorded on the right side of an account
A simple two-sided form used to analyse an account
The side on which an account usually carries its balance
Recording every transaction with equal debits and credits
An account whose normal balance opposes its related account
Journalizing and Posting: Journal
The book of original entry where transactions are first recorded
Journalizing
The act of recording a transaction in the journal
General journal
An all-purpose journal recording any transaction
Special journal
A journal dedicated to one repetitive transaction type
Ledger
The collection of all accounts and their balances
General ledger
The ledger holding all permanent and temporary accounts
Subsidiary ledger
A detailed ledger supporting a single control account
Posting
Transferring journal entries into ledger accounts
Posting reference
A notation linking a journal line to its ledger account
Compound entry
A journal entry affecting more than two accounts
Correcting entry
An entry made to fix a previously recorded mistake
Audit trail
The documented path allowing any figure to be traced to its source
The Trial Balance: Trial balance
A listing of all ledger accounts proving debits equal credits
Unadjusted trial balance
The trial balance prepared before adjusting entries
Adjusted trial balance
The trial balance prepared after adjustments are posted
Post-closing trial balance
The trial balance prepared after closing entries
Out of balance
A condition where total debits do not equal total credits
Transposition error
Reversing digits, producing a difference divisible by nine
Slide error
Misplacing a decimal point when recording an amount
Worksheet
A columnar tool organising trial balance, adjustments, and statements
Limitation of a trial balance
It cannot detect an entry posted to the wrong account
Footing
Adding a column of figures in an account
Ruling an account
Drawing a line to indicate a total or a closed account
Adjusting Entries: Adjusting entry
An entry updating accounts to reflect the correct period amounts
Accrual basis accounting
Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred
Cash basis accounting
Recording revenue and expenses only when cash moves
Matching principle
Recording expenses in the same period as the revenue they help produce
Revenue recognition principle
Recording revenue when it is earned, not when cash arrives
Accrued revenue
Revenue earned but not yet received or recorded
Accrued expense
An expense incurred but not yet paid or recorded
Prepaid expense
An asset representing payment made in advance of use
Unearned revenue
A liability representing cash received before the work is done
Depreciation
Allocating the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life
Accumulated depreciation
The contra-asset total of depreciation recorded to date
Book value
An asset's original cost minus accumulated depreciation
Straight-line depreciation
Spreading cost evenly across the asset's useful life
Financial Statements: A report of revenues and expenses over a period
The amount by which revenue exceeds expenses
The amount by which expenses exceed revenue
A report showing changes in the owner's claim over a period
A report of assets, liabilities, and equity at a single date
A report classifying cash movement into operating, investing, and financing
An asset expected to be converted to cash within one year
A long-lived tangible asset used in operations
An obligation due within one year
An obligation due beyond one year
The span of time a financial statement covers
A vertical balance sheet layout versus a side-by-side layout
Closing Entries: An entry that zeroes out temporary accounts at period end
An account closed each period, such as revenue or expense
A balance sheet account carried forward between periods
A temporary account used to gather revenue and expense totals
Debiting revenue and crediting income summary
Crediting expenses and debiting income summary
Transferring net income into the owner's capital account
The repeating sequence from transaction through closing
Resetting temporary accounts so the next period starts at zero
Capital increases by net income and decreases by withdrawals
Cash Control and Bank Reconciliation: Internal control
Procedures protecting assets and ensuring accurate records
Separation of duties
Dividing tasks so no one person controls a whole process
Bank reconciliation
Comparing the bank statement to the company's cash records
Outstanding check
A check written but not yet cleared by the bank
Deposit in transit
A deposit recorded by the company but not yet by the bank
Bank service charge
A fee the bank deducts, requiring a company journal entry
NSF check
A customer check returned for insufficient funds
Petty cash fund
A small cash reserve for minor expenditures
Replenishing petty cash
Restoring the fund to its fixed balance and recording expenses
Endorsement
A signature transferring ownership of a check
Blank versus restrictive endorsement
An open signature versus one limiting the check to deposit only
Electronic funds transfer
Moving money electronically without paper documents
Payroll Accounting: The total compensation a business pays its employees
Amounts an employer deducts and remits on the employee's behalf
Income tax deducted based on earnings and allowances
Social Security and Medicare taxes shared by employer and employee
A record summarising a pay period for all employees
A running annual record of one employee's pay and deductions
A fixed periodic amount versus pay based on hours worked
Premium pay, usually time and a half beyond forty hours
Taxes such as unemployment insurance paid by the employer alone
The annual statement of an employee's earnings and withholdings
The form an employee files to set withholding amounts
Merchandising Operations: Merchandising business
A business that buys finished goods and resells them
Merchandise inventory
Goods held for resale to customers
Cost of merchandise sold
The cost of the inventory that was actually sold
Gross profit
Net sales minus cost of merchandise sold
Purchases account
The account recording merchandise bought for resale
Purchases discount
A reduction for paying a supplier invoice early
Purchases return and allowance
A credit for returned or defective merchandise
Sales discount
A reduction offered to a customer for prompt payment
Sales return and allowance
A contra-revenue account for customer returns
Credit terms 2/10 n/30
Two percent off within ten days, full amount due in thirty
FOB shipping point
Ownership and freight cost transfer to the buyer at shipment
FOB destination
The seller retains ownership and freight cost until delivery
Net sales
Gross sales minus returns, allowances, and discounts
Inventory Methods: Perpetual inventory system
Continuously updating inventory records with each sale
Periodic inventory system
Updating inventory only after a physical count
Physical inventory
An actual count of goods on hand
FIFO method
Assuming the earliest goods purchased are sold first
LIFO method
Assuming the most recent goods purchased are sold first
Weighted average method
Valuing inventory at the average cost of all units available
FIFO in rising prices
Produces higher reported net income and higher ending inventory
LIFO in rising prices
Produces lower reported net income and lower taxes
Lower of cost or market
Writing inventory down when its market value falls below cost
Inventory turnover
How many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period
Effect of inventory error
An error in ending inventory misstates both income and equity
Consistency principle
Using the same inventory method from period to period
